entries.english:
CCLXXXIII. Emperor Charles IV confirms several possessions of the Church of Breslau, especially its liberties, and permits the church to lay out demesnes as villages under German law and to convert villages into demesnes. From the original in the cathedral chapter archive, C. 30. Only the black and white silk cords from which the lost seal hung remain.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, amen. Charles IV, by divine favor ever august Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, for perpetual remembrance. Almighty God, of supreme goodness, distributes rewards to each virtue through His ineffable goodness and is not accustomed to leave any good deed without the grace of a reward. Yet He honors those virtues which serve divine worship with a gift of reward all the more abundant, inasmuch as spiritual things are rightly preferred to temporal ones. Accordingly, mindful of the outstanding acts of devotion shown by our venerable faithful Preczslai, bishop and chancellor of the Church of Breslau, and by the canons and chapter of that church, who have endeavored with due affection to honor our majesty and our dearest father, the late illustrious John, formerly King of Bohemia, we have deliberately resolved—not in error or thoughtlessly, but with the sound counsel of our princes, barons, and nobles—to renew, approve, and, by royal authority in Bohemia and with certain knowledge, confirm in these letters all privileges, graces, liberties, and indulgences granted to them and to that church by our majesty, by our dearest father John, formerly King of Bohemia, or by any of our predecessors, the dukes of Silesia and lords of Breslau, counts, and barons. Whatever their content and extent, we confirm them as valid and approved, following the example of our father, who is known to have done the same.

Furthermore, as a special grace of royal kindness and in view of divine reward, we freely grant, bestow, and confer anew complete and unrestricted liberty upon the aforesaid bishop, chapter, clergy, and individual members of the Church of Breslau, including its dignitaries and officeholders, in the bishop’s villages—Krincz; Swauth or Bysschoffdorph; Turow; Radoschkouicz or Byskupicz; Shedlacouicz; and Jelin—as well as in the villages of his vassals, namely Ozoriez, Jeschkotel, and Pilzicz; in the chapter’s villages, namely Repelin, Suchalicz, Milowicz, Operou, Striganonicz, and Procan; in the provost’s village of Oltaczin; in the dean’s village of Mochobor; and in all their other properties, villages, demesnes, and appurtenances. We reserve no right, jurisdiction, tax, or service for ourselves, our heirs, or our successors.

Moreover, we graciously favor and grant to the bishop, chapter, and individual members of the Church of Breslau named above, and to their successors in office, the right to lay out their demesnes situated in our lands, in whole or in part, as villages under German law, and conversely to turn villages into demesnes and reduce them to that status, as they or any of them see fit. In either case, whether villages are made from demesnes or demesnes from villages, they shall enjoy forever the complete and unrestricted liberty set out above.

In addition, we promise in good faith to the aforesaid bishop and chapter that neither we nor our successors and heirs, the Kings of Bohemia, will ever burden the bishop, chapter, clergy of the Church of Breslau, or any lay subjects of ours residing within our domain and on the properties and possessions of that church with demands for money, animals, grain, services, transport, payments, tallages, levies, collections, compulsory services, extraordinary services, or any charges by whatever name they are called, nor with lodging or quartering in the villages and demesnes of the bishop, chapter, and church. We will preserve them and their possessions in full liberty, protect them, and defend them to the best of our ability.

Let no one infringe this charter of our majesty or dare to oppose it recklessly, under penalty of our severe displeasure; anyone who presumes to do so shall know that he incurs that displeasure gravely. Sign of the most serene prince and lord, Lord Charles IV, invincible and most glorious Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia.

Witnesses to this act are the venerable Ernest, Archbishop of the Holy Church of Prague; John, Bishop of Olomouc; Albert, Bishop of Schwerin; and Dietrich, Bishop of Minden; the illustrious William, Margrave of Meissen; Boleslaus of Świdnica; Conrad of Oleśnica; Wenceslaus and Louis of Legnica; Przemysław of Cieszyn; Boleslaus of Opole and Boleslaus of Falkenberg, dukes; the distinguished Burkhard and John, burgraves of Magdeburg; counts and nobles; Sbinko of Hasenburg, our supreme chamberlain; Jodocus and Johannes, brothers of Rosenberg; Sdenco of Sternberg, judge of the royal court in Bohemia; and many other of our princes, nobles, and faithful men. In witness of these letters, our imperial majesty’s seal is attached. Given at Breslau in the year of the Lord 1358, in the eleventh indiction, on the Ides of December, the thirteenth year of our reign and the fourth of our empire.

[Editorial notes: The emperor’s monogram appears here. The places numbered 2–5, 7, 11–12, and 17–18 had already been confirmed by the charter of 13 August 1345, no. CCLXXV. No. 6 is Schiedlagwitz, southwest of Breslau; no. 8 is now Oderwitz, southeast of Breslau; no. 9 is Jäschgüttel, southwest of Breslau, to which Polish Neudorf belonged; no. 10 is Pilsnitz, northwest of Breslau; no. 12 is Tschauchelwitz, southwest of Breslau; no. 13 is Mellowitz, southeast of Breslau; no. 14 is Opperau, southwest of Breslau; no. 15 is now Paschwitz, southwest of Breslau; and no. 16 is Protsch an der Weide, northwest of Breslau. The earlier confirmations are King John’s charters of 4 October 1342, no. CCLXX, and 13 August 1345, no. CCLXXV.]
